Its range is wide, spanning three and a half to six octaves, from a deep resonance to a high brightness, and it can express many layers of music. When wet fingertips rub the glass rods the sound is clear and pure as crystal, with a subtle vibrato. The instrument sounds through the resonance of the glass rods themselves, in a distinctive way: the timbre sits between the electronic synthesiser and string instruments, with the carrying power of the piano and the graceful singing of the violin, yet more unreal and dreamlike. This unusual sounding mechanism gives the instrument acoustic qualities without precedent and makes it an ideal choice for contemporary classical and experimental music.

水晶琴於1952年由法國樂器製作者Bernard和François Basche: The Cristal Baschet was developed in 1952 by the French instrument makers Bernard and François Baschet. It sounds when wet fingers rub glass rods, and the vibration is transformed and amplified through metal rods, glass-fibre cones and flame-shaped metal pieces. It was first used for musique concrète, and later players such as Jacques and Yvonne Lasry and Michel Deneuve developed technique and repertoire for it. In 1993 a workshop opened at the Albi Conservatoire, in 2003 a class was set up at the Brive-la-Gaillarde Conservatoire, and from 2010 it has been run by Antoine Mas; it has entered dance, film music, theatre, jazz, improvisation, contemporary music, fado, song and rock.

The amplifying parts include glass-fibre cones, a wooden frame and flame-shaped cut metal pieces. The whiskers at the side, which amplify the high notes, are of unstated material. The rest of the body's structure is also unstated.

Players include Jacques and Yvonne Lasry, Michel Deneuve, Thomas Bloch and Dennis James; composers include François Bayle, Luc Ferrari, Toru Takemitsu, Jean Michel Jarre and Cliff Martinez. The Cristal Baschet is an idiophone created in 1952 by the French Baschet brothers, Hornbostel–Sachs number 131.2, in the same line as the glass harmonica. It uses 56 chromatically tuned glass rods connected to metal rods set into a thick plate; the length, weight and balance point of the metal rods determine the pitch. The player sounds it by rubbing the glass rods with wet fingertips, and the vibration passes through the metal parts to the glass-fibre cones in a wooden frame and to flame-shaped metal pieces that amplify it, while fine whiskers at the side reinforce the high notes. It was first used for musique concrète, and later entered dance, film music, theatre, jazz, improvisation, contemporary music, fado, song and rock, and was promoted by players such as Lasry, Deneuve, Bloch and James.
